units.summary: Rav relates that he found a hidden scroll in the house of Rabbi Hiyya containing a teaching by Isi ben Yehuda regarding the thirty-nine prohibited labors of Shabbat.
Shmuel instructs Rav Yehuda not to concern himself with the laws of karmelit above ten handbreadths.
Rav Yehuda describes a case of someone repeatedly lifting and dropping a bundle of reeds to determine liability for carrying.
Rava sees Rav Hamnuna praying at length and rebukes him for prioritizing prayer over Torah study.
Rav Ḥisda holds priestly gifts and offers them to anyone who can tell him a new teaching of Rav, which Rava bar Meḥasseya then does.
Rav Yehoshua son of Rav Idi visits Rav Ashi and declines a high-quality meal because he is observing a fast.
Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha attempted to read by candlelight on Shabbat, nearly adjusted the wick, and subsequently wrote a note testifying that the Sages' prohibition was justified.
Ulla used to kiss his sisters upon returning from the house of his teacher.

A diligent student dies young, leading his widow to carry his tefillin to study halls and demand an explanation for his premature death. The wife of a student who died young seeks an explanation for his death until Eliyahu the Prophet visits her and investigates the matter.
Hananya ben Hizkiya prevents the suppression of the Book of Ezekiel by isolating himself in an attic with 300 jars of oil to resolve its legal contradictions.
Rabbi Tarfon begins to comment on a halakhic tradition regarding the impurity transmitted by an ox goad.
During a heated debate between Hillel and Shammai, a sword was stuck in the study hall to force a vote, resulting in Hillel's physical submission to Shammai.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel describes the habitual practice of his father's house regarding giving laundry to a gentile before Shabbat.
Abaye brings a dyed garment to a launderer and rebukes him when the launderer tries to charge the same high price as for a white garment.
A student issued a ruling according to Rabbi Shimon in the jurisdiction of Rav, and Rav Hamnuna excommunicated him for it.
A man was heard offering 'achvana' for sale, and it was discovered that he was referring to willow branches, resolving a dispute between Rav and Shmuel.
While sitting before Rabbana Neḥemya, Ravin observes his silk garment and attempts to identify it as the 'kalakh' mentioned in the Mishna, leading to a brief debate with Abaye.
Ravin and Abaye walk through the Valley of Tamrurita and identify certain willow trees as the 'idan' mentioned in the Mishna.
Abaye initially rejects a legal ruling when cited in the name of Rabbi Yirmeya but accepts it when Ravin cites it in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan.
Two elders in Sidon followed different practices regarding Hanukkah lights, one following Beit Shammai and the other Beit Hillel.
The Gemara recounts the miracle of Hanukkah: the Hasmoneans defeated the Greeks, found a single pure jar of oil that miraculously lasted eight days, and established the holiday.

Passage B contains two distinct narrative incidents involving Rav Huna and Rav Hisda observing the lighting habits of families and predicting the birth of scholars, which is a different narrative unit from the story of Rav Yosef's wife in Passage A.
Rav Yosef observes his wife lighting Shabbat lamps late and instructs her to light earlier by citing the biblical precedent of the pillars of cloud and fire.
A mother-in-law who hated her daughter-in-law tricked her into using volatile balsam oil and lighting a lamp, causing her to catch fire.
Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri stands up to protest a ruling by asking what people in other regions with different oils should do.
Rav ate dates and threw the pits into an oven on a weekday, leading Rabbi Ḥiyya to warn him that doing so on a Festival would be prohibited.
When Rav arrived in Babylonia, he ate dates on a Festival and threw the pits to animals.
Rabbi Yehuda recounts a time he and other sages used a perforated eggshell filled with oil to fuel a lamp on Shabbat in Lod.
Avin of Tzippori dragged a bench on a marble floor in front of Rabbi Yitzḥak ben Elazar, who then rebuked him by comparing the silence of other sages to his own potential silence.
The head of the synagogue in Batzra dragged a bench before Rabbi Yirmeya, who challenged the legality of his action.
Rabbi Tanḥum is asked a legal question about Shabbat and begins a long homiletical response.
David asks God to reveal when he will die, and though God refuses to reveal the exact date, He reveals that David will die on a Shabbat.
Following David's death, Solomon consults the Sages on how to handle his father's body on Shabbat, and they instruct him to use a loaf of bread to allow the body to be moved.
A man comes before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi with an insulting claim, and after drinking wine offered by the Rabbi, he physically bursts.
When a student scoffs at Rabban Gamliel's teaching that women will give birth daily in the future, the Rabbi shows him a hen as a current example of daily birth.
Rabban Gamliel responds to a student's skepticism regarding trees bearing fruit daily by showing him a caper bush.
Rabban Gamliel proves to a scoffing student that the earth can produce ready-to-eat food by showing him mushrooms and truffles.

Two men wager four hundred zuz on whether one of them can make Hillel the Elder lose his temper. A man attempts to win a wager by repeatedly annoying Hillel on the eve of Shabbat with trivial questions, but Hillel's extreme patience causes the man to lose his money.
A gentile asks Shammai to convert him based only on the Written Torah, and Shammai rebukes him.
Shammai physically ejects a gentile who asks to be taught the entire Torah while standing on one foot.
A gentile who initially seeks conversion only to become High Priest is guided by Hillel through study to realize his own limitations, eventually becoming a sincere convert.
Rabbi Simon and Rabbi Elazar see Rabbi Ya’akov bar Aḥa passing and debate whether to stand for him based on his fear of sin or his Torah knowledge.
Rav would avoid crossing a river in a ferry containing a gentile to avoid shared divine judgment.
Rabbi Yannai would inspect ferries for structural integrity before crossing to avoid relying on miracles.
Shmuel HaKatan falls ill with hidrokan and prays for healing so that people do not assume he sinned, and he is subsequently cured.

After being sentenced to death by the Romans for criticizing their infrastructure, Rabbi Shimon bar Yohai and his son hide in a cave for thirteen years, undergo a spiritual and physical transformation, and eventually return to society. Rabbi Shimon bar Yoḥai uses testimony from an elder to purify a suspected cemetery for the benefit of the priests, and subsequently rebukes an elder who mocks his ruling.
Abaye observes Rava looking toward the west on Shabbat eve to determine the time and questions him based on a baraita regarding the signs of twilight.
Rava instructs his attendant to light the Shabbat lamp as soon as he sees the sun atop the trees, rather than waiting for the stars.
The Baraita describes the habitual procedure of sounding six shofar blasts to usher in the Shabbat and the corresponding cessation of work by the public.

Rav Yosef cites the fact that food was left on the stove for Rav Yehuda and he ate it as evidence for the permissibility of the practice, though Abaye argues this was only due to Rav Yehuda's medical danger.
A legal dilemma is posed to Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba.
Rabbi Yosei travels to Tzippori and finds people leaving water and eggs on the fire, leading him to permit the water but forbid the eggs.
Rav Ḥama bar Ḥanina recounts a time he and Rabbi Judah HaNasi were served and ate many small, well-cooked eggs while being hosted.
Rav Oshaya recounts a time when he and others were standing before Rabbi Hiyya on Shabbat and passed him a kettle of hot water.
The people of Tiberias constructed a pipe system to heat cold water using hot springs, but the Sages ruled the resulting water prohibited on Shabbat.
The people of Tiberias attempted to heat cold water by running it through hot springs in a pipe, but the Sages prohibited the practice.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and Rabbi Akiva entered a sealed bathhouse on a Festival to sweat and rinse, an act that led to a subsequent rabbinic prohibition.
The Gemara describes how bathhouse attendants' deceptive practice of heating water on Shabbat led the Sages to prohibit hot water bathing entirely.
Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Avdimi attempts to heat oil for Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi in a bathhouse, but the Rabbi instructs him to use a secondary vessel to avoid a Shabbat violation.
A student of Rabbi Meir attempts to rinse the floor and oil his teacher in a bathhouse, but Rabbi Meir stops him from performing these actions.

Rabbi Zeira observes Rabbi Abbahu floating in a bathhouse on Shabbat but is unsure if he was technically swimming. Rabbi Zeira observes Rabbi Abbahu's modest physical conduct while bathing in the bathhouse.
Rabbi Zeira avoids his teacher Rav Yehuda to move to Israel, but follows him to a bathhouse where he overhears Rav Yehuda's mundane requests and derives halakhic permissions from them.
Rav Huna reports observing that Rava was not strict about placing vessels in hot or cold water, citing a baraita as the source for this leniency.
When Zoroastrian priests threatened to seize Hanukkah lamps, Rav permitted moving the lamps on Shabbat to hide them.
Rabbi Shimon asks his father, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, a legal question about set-aside dates.
Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Assi visit Rabbi Abba of Haifa, and a candelabrum falls onto their clothing, creating a dilemma about moving it on Shabbat.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi travels to Deyosfera and issues a legal ruling regarding a candelabrum.
Rav Malkiya and Rabbi Yosei the Galilean visit other rabbis and move lamps, causing their hosts to become angry.
Rav Avya arrives at Rava's house with muddy feet and sits on his bed, leading an angry Rava to attempt to embarrass him with difficult legal questions.
Rabbi Romanus reports that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi permitted him to move a coal pan, leading to a confrontation where Rabbi Asi is momentarily silenced by a contradiction.
Levi bar Shmuel finds two rabbis at a doorway and asks them a legal question about weaver's looms.
In the house of Rav Hama, they used to reassemble a collapsible bed on Festivals, leading a sage to question Rava on the legal basis for the practice.
Rabba and Rabbi Zeira visit the Exilarch's house and Rabba repeatedly rebukes a servant for his methods of heating and covering water vessels on Shabbat.
Elisha defies a Roman decree against wearing phylacteries and, when pursued by an official, his phylacteries miraculously turn into dove wings, saving his life.
Rabbis sit together to discuss whether the Mishna's ruling on hides applies to craftsmen or only homeowners.
A sage recalls his father, a tanner, telling the family to bring hides to sit on during Shabbat.
A new student in the study hall raises a legal objection to Rava's ruling regarding wool fleece.
Rabbi Hanina ben Akiva once went to a certain place and sat on palm branches that had not been tied together before Shabbat.

Ameimar, Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi are presented with a washing mixture on Shabbat; Ameimar and Rav Ashi use it while Mar Zutra refuses, leading to a discussion of their conflicting halakhic rationales.
Rav Nahman instructs his slave Daru to insulate cold food and bring water heated by a gentile, which causes Rabbi Ami to become angry when he hears of it.
Levi sends money to buy a Libyan donkey, but the sellers return his money along with barley to signal that a donkey's quality depends on its feed.

While traveling, Levi's donkey overtakes Rabba bar Rav Huna's donkey, causing Rabba to feel slighted by the perceived breach of etiquette. While traveling, Levi's donkey overtakes Rabba bar Rav Huna's donkey, causing offense, which Levi then attempts to resolve by asking a legal question to show respect.
Rav Yosef observes the practice of Rav Huna's household regarding how their calves go out on Shabbat.
Rabbis arriving from Eretz Yisrael report on the habitual practice of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's household regarding their mules on Shabbat.
A disciple from the Upper Galilee approaches Rabbi Eliezer to clarify traditions he heard regarding distinctions between types of rings and needles.
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Yosef reports Rav's lenient ruling on fodder baskets to Shmuel, who responds by questioning Rav's knowledge of Shabbat laws.
Rabbi Zeira travels to Eretz Yisrael and hears Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet quoting Rabbi Yoḥanan, noting that it aligns with Shmuel's (Aryokh's) view in Babylonia.
The residents of Antioch made pouches for their goats to prevent their large udders from dragging and getting scratched.
A man married a one-armed woman and, due to her extreme modesty, never realized her condition until she passed away.

The Talmud explains that the cow famously associated with Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's violation of Shabbat actually belonged to his neighbor, but was attributed to him because he failed to protest her actions.
While Rav Yehuda is sitting before Shmuel, a woman cries out for justice, and Rav Yehuda rebukes Shmuel for ignoring her.
Rabbi Zeira urges Rabbi Simon to rebuke the members of the Exilarch's household, but Rabbi Simon demurs, claiming they will not listen.
In a heavenly dialogue, the Attribute of Justice convinces God to punish the righteous along with the wicked because they failed to protest the sins of their generation.
Rav Yosef recounts a dream he had while dozing at a lecture in which a hand from heaven reached out to accept the repentance of Okvan bar Neḥemya.
Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua reports that his sisters do not mind the woven chains in their hair and consequently immerse in the ritual bath without removing them.
Shmuel instructs Rav Hinnana bar Sheila that he is exempt from the restriction against wearing sealed cloaks on Shabbat because the Exilarch's household is not particular with him.
The Gemara mentions that Rabbi Akiva made a 'city of gold' ornament for his wife.
Rav identifies a mysterious limping scholar in Nehardea as Levi and uses his presence there to deduce that Rabbi Afes has died.
When Levi and Rabba bar Avuh permitted the kelila ornament, large numbers of women in their respective cities immediately began wearing them in public.

During a period of persecution, a group hiding in a cave panics due to misleading footprints from a spiked sandal, leading to a stampede where they kill each other, which results in a ban on wearing such sandals on Shabbat.
A shoemaker asks Rabbi Ami about the status of a sandal sewn from within, and the Rabbi permits it without knowing the reason.
Rabbi Yoḥanan asks his attendant for a sandal and rebukes him for bringing the right one first, implying it makes his foot seem wounded.
Rav Ḥisda reports that because he was meticulous in using large amounts of water for ritual hand-washing, he was rewarded with great prosperity.
The Gemara describes how the arrogant people of Jerusalem used euphemisms to discuss their meals and social habits.
Rav Kahana reflects on how he had mastered the entire Talmud by age eighteen but only recently realized the principle that scripture never loses its literal meaning.
A pregnant woman miscarries after being frightened by a barking dog, and she rebukes the owner's claim that the dog was harmless by noting the damage is already done.
A family in Jerusalem whose daughters suffered injuries from over-striding created ankle chains to limit their steps and protect them.
Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Yosei reports seeing the High Priest's frontplate in Rome and describes its inscription.
Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Yannai are reported to have walked into public domains with cloths in their ears, prompting disagreement from their peers.
Shmuel's father enforced specific modesty rules for his daughters and physically constructed ritual baths for them in the river during specific seasons.
Shmuel's father took several physical and restrictive measures to ensure the ritual purity and modesty of his daughters, including building specific ritual baths and laying mats in the river.
A tanna recites a version of a mishna before Rabbi Yoḥanan, who corrects him and insists on a different reading based on legal logic.
When Rav Huna, Rav, and Rabbi Ḥiyya would leave their respective teachers' homes in a state of intoxication, the teachers would rub oil and salt on them as a remedy.
Rabbi Akiva hosted a banquet for his son and repeatedly recited a blessing of 'wine and life' over every cup served to demonstrate it was not a forbidden Amorite practice.
Rav Dimi reports an incident where Rav Beivai served fruit to Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi without removing the stems, illustrating a practical application of the laws of selecting on Shabbat.
Rabbi Zeira encounters Rav Yehuda in a particularly good mood and takes the opportunity to ask him a series of questions about the names and nature of various creatures and objects.
Rav Beivai successfully beautified his daughter with lime, but when his gentile neighbor attempted to do the same all at once, his daughter died.
Zunin enters the study hall to ask about the size of stones for the bathroom and, after mocking the Sages' overly specific answer, prompts them to vote and change the law to a more practical measure.
While traveling on a boat, Rav Hisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna refuse a matron's request to join them, leading to a magical duel where she stops the boat and they release it.
Rav Huna questions his son Rabba on why he avoids Rav Hisda's lectures, and Rabba explains that he finds Rav Hisda's focus on anatomy and hygiene to be 'mundane matters.'
The Gemara lists three actions Moses took based on his own reasoning, such as breaking the tablets and separating from his wife, which God later approved.
The page consists of a complex chronological and legal debate between various Amoraim regarding the exact dates and days of the week for the Exodus and the Revelation at Sinai.
A heretic mocks Rava for being so engrossed in study that he doesn't notice his own fingers bleeding, leading to a debate about the impulsiveness versus the integrity of the Jewish people.

When Moses ascends to heaven to receive the Torah, the angels object to a mortal's presence, leading God to instruct a fearful Moses to hold onto the Divine Throne for protection while he answers them. Moses successfully defends humanity's right to the Torah against the angels, who then become his friends and give him gifts.
Satan searches the universe for the Torah and eventually finds it with Moses, whose humility leads God to name the Torah after him.
Moses encounters God tying crowns to the letters of the Torah and is prompted by God to offer a greeting.
Satan uses the delay in Moses' return to deceive the Israelites with a vision of his death, leading to the sin of the Golden Calf.
Shmuel recounts how he questioned seafarers to identify the substance 'eshlag' mentioned in the Mishna.
Rav Kahana was standing before Rav and passed a locust over his mouth, leading Rav to tell him to remove it so people wouldn't think he was eating it.
A Tanna recites a legal tradition regarding two people carrying a reed before Rav Nahman, who corrects the attribution of the opinions.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak permits the removal of a corpse to a karmelit in the city of Derokera on Shabbat, leading to a brief legal challenge by Rabbi Yoḥanan.
Rav Naḥman bar Gurya visits Neharde’a and answers a series of legal questions regarding prohibited labors on Shabbat.
Ameimar permits sprinkling water on the floors in Meḥoza because the floors are paved, and Rava Tosfa'a observes Ravina's distress.
An elder asks Rabbi Zeira a legal question about perforated pots, and after initial silence, Rabbi Zeira is later found teaching the resolution.
Rav relates how he found a hidden scroll in the house of Rabbi Hiyya containing a teaching by Isi ben Yehuda regarding the thirty-nine labors.

Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira rebukes Rabbi Akiva for identifying the anonymous wood-gatherer as Zelophehad, warning him he will be held accountable for either slandering a righteous man or revealing what the Torah concealed.
A baraita mentions that the middle bar of the Tabernacle stood miraculously.
Rav Mordekhai travels between Rava, Rav Yosef, and Abaye asking the same legal question, eventually rebuking them all for providing the same answer from the Mishna.
Rav Natan bar Oshaya asks Rabbi Yoḥanan about the category of labor for chiseling, and Rabbi Yoḥanan gestures with his hand to indicate it is 'striking with a hammer.'
Young students arrive at the study hall and amaze the Sages with novel homiletic interpretations of the Hebrew alphabet, which are then reported to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.
Rabbi Eliezer cites the case of Ben Stada, who smuggled magic spells out of Egypt by scratching them onto his skin.

The Gemara records the specific methods used by Rav Yehuda, Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov, and Rav Sheshet to perform acts of 'anger' (like breaking things or throwing brine) to discipline their households without actually violating prohibitions or causing real damage.
Shmuel and Karna encounter Rav arriving from Eretz Yisrael, leading to a series of tests, curses, and a medical intervention by Shmuel to treat Rav's ailment.
A Boethusian challenges Rabbi Yehoshua HaGarsi regarding the source for using only kosher skins for phylacteries.
While Bar Liva’ei was standing before Mar Ukva on Shabbat, he observed Mar Ukva applying eye salve in a specific manner, which Mar Ukva then justified based on Shmuel's teaching.
Ze'iri's wife prepares melon juice for Hiyya bar Ashi, and when he refuses to drink it, she points out that his own teacher used to drink it.
After a donkey steps on Rav Ashi's foot, Ravina observes him treating it with vinegar (or wine) on Shabbat and questions the legality of the act.
Ulla visits Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda and is presented with hyssop, leading to a discussion on its identification.
The mother of Rav Ahadvoi bar Ami treats a man who swallowed venom by having him drink a potion and sit on a heated brick, resulting in the venom being expelled.

Rav Shimi bar Ashi saves a man who swallowed a snake by feeding him a remedy and forcing him to run behind a horseman (Rav Ashi), causing the snake to be expelled. A Jewish official in Pumbedita is bitten by a snake, but the attempt to cure him using white donkeys fails because they are either unfit or eaten by a lion.
An Arab suffering from jaundice trades his cloak for leeks, eats them, and sleeps in the gardener's cloak until he sweats out the illness and is cured.
While walking behind Rabbi Abbahu on Shabbat, Rabbi Yirmeya's sandal strap breaks, and Rabbi Abbahu instructs him to bind it with a moist reed.
Rabbi Yoḥanan corrects his teacher Ḥizkiya by citing Ḥizkiya's own previous ruling, leading Ḥizkiya to praise him as an angel.
The household of Rabban Gamliel had a custom not to fold their white garments on Shabbat because they had replacements available.
The Gemara analyzes the actions of Ruth and Boaz, focusing on Ruth's modesty while gleaning and her obedience to Naomi.
Abba Halafta visits Rabban Gamliel and, upon seeing him reading a translation of Job, reminds him of a precedent, leading Gamliel to order the book buried in a wall.
Passage B introduces a new baraita containing a distinct narrative incident involving Rabbi Yishmael and a scribe in Sidon, which is separate from the legal debate in Passage A.

Imma Shalom and her brother Rabban Gamliel plot to expose a local philosopher's hypocrisy regarding bribery. Imma Shalom and Rabban Gamliel use competing bribes of a lamp and a donkey to expose the hypocrisy of a local philosopher who claimed to be incorruptible.
Rav Ashi observes Rav Kahana's specific physical practice of holding two loaves but breaking only one, while Rabbi Zeira's habit of breaking a large piece is also noted.
While climbing a staircase, Rabba's ritual fringe broke, and he refused to move until it was fixed.
Yosef, known for honoring Shabbat, acquires the entire fortune of a gentile neighbor who tried to hide his wealth in a gem after astrologers predicted Yosef would eventually possess it.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba visits a wealthy man in Laodicea who displays a magnificent golden table and explains his wealth is a reward for honoring Shabbat.
The Roman Emperor asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya for the secret spice that makes Shabbat food smell so good, only to be told it only works for those who observe the day.
A sage would seek out pairs of scholars talking on Shabbat and exhort them to ensure they were properly delighting in the day.
Yosef ben Simai refuses to let gentile soldiers extinguish a fire in his courtyard on Shabbat, leading to a miraculous rain that puts out the flames.
Passage B contains a Mishnaic incident involving Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai and a specific ruling on a scorpion, which is distinct from the Gemara's narrative in Passage A.

Three rabbis visit Avin of Nashikiya, but the host only provides beds for two of them, causing the third to feel slighted. Rav Ḥanan bar Rava, insulted that his host Avin did not provide him a bed, angrily interrupts Avin's lesson to his son and calls his teaching foolish.
A snake falls into the study hall on Shabbat and is killed by a Nabatean, prompting a cryptic remark from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
While being tormented by the Exilarch's men for a debt on Shabbat, Abba bar Marta spits, leading the Exilarch to order it covered with a bowl.
Rabban Gamliel and his companions use a ramp built by a gentile on Shabbat to disembark from their ship, justifying it because the ramp was not built specifically for them.

Shmuel visits a home where a gentile lights a lamp, and after initially turning away to avoid a forbidden benefit, he realizes the gentile lit it for his own reading and thus permits himself to use the light.
Rabba initially intended to answer Abaye's objection using one legal theory but changed his mind after hearing a different tradition from Rav Hinana bar Shelemya.
Rav Kahana visits Rav's house, and Rav instructs his attendants to bring or move a net for Kahana to sit on.
Rav Mari bar Raḥel asks Rava if he may move his felt cushions out of the sun on Shabbat, and Rava provides a permissive ruling.
While Rava is walking in Meḥoza, his servant uses a shard to clean mud off Rava's shoes, prompting a protest from other Sages which Rava rebuffs.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi visited a place, found a stack of stones, and instructed the people to perform a physical action on them so they could be used as seats on Shabbat.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi (or Rabbi Hiyya) finds a study location too crowded for his students, so he goes to a nearby field and clears bundles of grain to make space for them.
A worker who was denied his wages for three years judges his employer favorably, only to have the employer later arrive at his home to pay him and explain the pious reasons for the delay.
A pious man redeems a captive woman and acts in a way that looks suspicious, but his students judge him favorably and are proven correct.
Rabbi Yehoshua visits a Roman matron on a political mission and performs several ambiguous acts, which his students correctly interpret in a favorable light.
An anonymous merchant offers 'koranita' for sale and is discovered to be selling thyme, which the Gemara uses to identify the plant.
Rav Yitzḥak bar Ami visits Rav Ḥisda and observes the household moving raw duck meat from the sun to the shade on Shabbat.
The daughter of Rav Hisda immersed in a ritual bath within thirty days of giving birth while her husband was away.

After undergoing bloodletting, various Sages had their expensive furniture broken to provide firewood for warmth, leading to a dialogue between Abaye and Rabba about the prohibition of wasteful destruction.
Ablat the scholar finds Shmuel lying in the sun and questions him, leading Shmuel to hide the medical secret of the Tammuz solstice by claiming it was merely for bloodletting recovery.
Shmuel, who usually performed bloodletting in a room with very thick walls, felt weak one day and discovered that a single half-brick was missing from the wall's thickness.
Rav Yosef recalls how students at Rav Huna's academy would cease their studies on days deemed dangerous for bloodletting.
Levi visits Yosef the hunter and is served peacock in milk, leading to a confrontation with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi about why he didn't excommunicate the household.
A city that followed Rabbi Eliezer's circumcision rulings was miraculously protected from early death and Roman decrees.
Elisha is pursued by a Roman official for wearing phylacteries, but when caught, the phylacteries miraculously turn into dove wings.
An incident where a circumcision scalpel was forgotten and subsequently brought on Shabbat via roofs and courtyards.
An incident is recounted where a scalpel was forgotten on Shabbat eve and subsequently transported through an unmerged alleyway to perform a circumcision.

When Rava publicly revealed a medical recipe in Meḥoza, the local doctors tore their clothes in despair over their lost livelihood, leading Rava to promise he would keep another medical secret private for their sake.
Rabbi Meir falls ill on Shabbat but refuses to let his students prepare a medicinal mixture for him, leading to a discussion on whether he is negating his own lenient ruling.
Rabbi Natan recounts how he saved a woman's third son by diagnosing that the baby was too 'red' for immediate circumcision, unlike her previous sons who died.
In a second incident, Rabbi Natan saves a baby in Cappadocia by identifying that its 'green' appearance indicated it was not yet healthy enough for circumcision.
A man brings a case to Rava regarding washing a baby after circumcision; Rava rules leniently but then falls ill, leading him to regret his decision and debate its textual basis with his students.
Rav Adda bar Ahava's son was born circumcised on Shabbat, and after thirteen circumcisors refused to perform the ritual, Rav Adda did it himself and accidentally maimed the child.
Rav Pappa and Rav Huna visit the son of Rav Idi bar Avin, who prepares a calf for them that was slaughtered on its eighth day.
When the son of Rav Dimi bar Yosef mourned for a child who died within thirty days of birth, his father rebuked him for performing an unnecessary ritual.
Rav Ashi visits Rav Kahana and finds him mourning for a child who died within thirty days, leading to a discussion on the halakha of viability.
Rav Yosef observes that in Rav Huna's house, canopies were spread in the evening and dismantled by morning, proving the permissibility of these actions on Shabbat.
Rami bar Yeḥezkel sends a message to Rav Huna asking him to repeat legal traditions he heard from Rav.
The Sages enter the vineyard at Yavne and declare that the Torah is destined to be forgotten.
The people of Bashkar send legal queries to Levi, but he dies while the messenger is en route, leading Shmuel to direct Rav Menashya to answer them.
It narrates a specific conflict between Rav's public announcement and Rav Amram Ḥasida's physical enforcement (lashes), involving different actors and a distinct outcome from the subsequent story.
Rav Mesharshiya would pay a gentile child to sow hops for him to avoid legal prohibitions.

An incident occurred in the synagogue of Maon where a person died on a Festival adjacent to Shabbat, leading to a query for Rabbi Yohanan. Following a death in the community of Maon on a Festival adjacent to Shabbat, the people consult Rabbi Yoḥanan, who instructs that gentiles may perform the burial.
The Rabbis report to Rav Ashi that Rav Huna used a piece of garlic as a makeshift plug/filter, and Rav Ashi defends the practice as a permissible form of artifice for a scholar.
The mothers and wives of sages prepare mustard on Shabbat, but their students/sons refuse to eat it, leading to a confrontation about their stringency.
Rav Yosef recounts how Mar Ukva gave him a medicinal drink after the bathhouse that was so potent he felt it throughout his entire body.
Rav Aha bar Yosef seeks medical advice for a heart condition from Mar Ukva, leading to a discussion of a previous incident where Rav Hiyya bar Avin sought a similar ruling.
Rav Aha bar Yosef, leaning on his nephew while walking, visits Rav Safra to ask about laundering a shirt on Shabbat and later explains the reasoning to his nephew.
Rav Ḥisda recounts his personal history of abstaining from eating vegetables during both his periods of poverty and wealth to manage his appetite and health.
Rav Ḥisda performs a physical demonstration for his daughters using a pearl and a clod of earth to teach them the value of modesty and mystery.
Abaye and Rava used spoons and knives to move muktzeh items on Shabbat, leading Rav Yosef to mock them and prompting their self-justifications.
Rava instructs his servant to roast a duck and feed the remains to a cat on a Festival.
Rav Safra recounts visiting Rabbi Abba and eating a specially prepared chicken that was so rich it would have endangered him had he not drunk wine.
Rav Gaza reports that on one occasion he visited a certain place and prepared a Babylonian kutaḥ dish.
While Rabbi Yoḥanan dozes, his students Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Asi converse, eventually waking him and prompting him to rebuke them for speaking without certainty.
The Gemara discusses the origin of moral contamination from the primordial snake and its removal at Mount Sinai or through the generations of the Patriarchs.
Rav and his students find no room in a certain place, so Rav sits in a carmelit but refuses to sit on felt cushions brought to him.

When Ulla visited Pumbedita and rebuked the local rabbis for shaking dust off their cloaks on Shabbat, Rav Yehuda told them to keep doing it in Ulla's presence to show they didn't care for his ruling.
Abaye hesitated to give Rav Yosef his hat because it had dew on it, but Rav Yosef told him to shake it off and throw it to him.
Hyrcanus son of Rabbi Eliezer went out on Shabbat with a scarf tied to his finger to prevent it from falling, and the Sages later permitted the practice.
Passage B describes a distinct event where Ulla visits a specific household and provides a ruling on a different legal question than the one discussed in Passage A.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi was walking in a field with his cloak on his shoulders when a student challenged him based on a ruling by Rabbi Meir or Rabbi Akiva, leading to a clarification of the law.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi recalls how he and his colleagues would carry oil and towels between roofs and courtyards while studying with Rabbi Shimon in Tekoa.
Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh visited a place of pleasure, forgot his Torah knowledge, and consequently misread a verse in the Torah scroll upon his return.
When Rabba bar bar Ḥana avoided Rav Yehuda's lecture in Pumbedita, Rav Yehuda sent his attendant to forcibly bring him there.
While Rav Avya was sitting before Rav Yosef, his hand became dislocated, and through the course of their interaction, it was healed.
A midrashic account of Nebuchadnezzar's physical transformation when he intended to harm Zedekiah.
A midrashic description of Nebuchadnezzar's arrival in Gehenna and the reaction of its inhabitants.
A pious man refrains from planning the repair of a breach in his field because it is Shabbat, and in reward, a miraculous caper bush grows to fill the gap and provide for his family.
A student of Rabbi Meir follows him into a bathhouse and is stopped by the Rabbi when he tries to rinse the floor on Shabbat.
Rabbi Hiyya instructs his wife to be quick in giving bread to the poor so that others will be quick to give to their children, explaining the cyclical nature of poverty.
When Rabbi Hanina's daughter dies, he refuses to weep, explaining to his critical wife that crying would cause him to go blind.
The Roman emperor asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya why he has not attended the House of Avidan, and the Rabbi responds with a series of metaphors describing the physical decline of old age.
An apostate eunuch mocks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa for his baldness and lack of shoes, leading to a sharp exchange of insults regarding their respective physical conditions.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asks Rabbi Shimon ben Ḥalafta why he did not visit during the festival, and Shimon explains how the physical toll of old age has made the journey impossible.
While Rav Kahana is reading verses to Rav, Rav sighs upon hearing a verse about old age, leading Rav Kahana to remark on Rav's loss of physical desire.

When a man in Rav Yehuda's neighborhood dies with no one to mourn him, Rav Yehuda organizes a group of ten to sit in his place for the week of mourning. Rav Yehuda organizes a minyan to sit in the home of a man who died without mourners, and after seven days, the deceased appears in his dream to thank him.
Diggers in Rav Nahman's field disturb the grave of Rav Ahai bar Yoshiya, leading to a physical encounter and dialogue between Rav Nahman and the miraculously preserved corpse.
An apostate challenges Rabbi Abbahu regarding the location of souls and the biblical story of Samuel and the necromancer.
Rav Adda bar Ahava provides a legal ruling regarding how one should proceed if they are carrying a package when Shabbat begins.
Rabban Gamliel's donkey, laden with honey, died at the end of Shabbat because he refused to unload it during the holy day.
Abaye observes Rabba sliding his son on a donkey on Shabbat and challenges the legality of the act.

Passage B follows the exact same literary formula as Passage A—citing a personal notebook entry involving a student questioning his rabbi—but features different actors (Ze’eiri and Rabbi Ḥiyya) and a distinct legal inquiry.
Levi reports to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that people in Babylonia knead shatit on Shabbat, causing the Rabbi to cry out in protest.
While it follows the same 'written in the notebook' formula as Passage A, it introduces a new actor (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) and a completely different subject matter (astrological/birth traits).
Abraham argues with God about his astrological inability to have children, and God tells him to transcend astrology.
Shmuel and the sage Ablet witness a man survive a predicted snakebite because he shared his bread with a hungry companion.
Rabbi Akiva's daughter escapes a predicted fatal snakebite on her wedding day by giving her food to a poor man.
The mother of Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak kept his head covered to prevent him from becoming a thief, but when his covering fell off one day, he immediately stole dates.
The Rabbis attended to Rav Zutra, the son of Rav Zeira, and dissolved his vow on Shabbat even though he had time to do so previously.
Ulla visits the Exilarch's house and observes Rabba bar Rav Huna measuring the water in his bathing tub on Shabbat, leading to a discussion on the permissibility of measuring.
